## 1. Categorical vs. Categorical: Substance Choice and Housing Status

### Research Question
For patients admitted to a clinical detoxification unit, is there a statistically significant association between their primary substance of abuse and their housing status?

### Data & Summary
```{r helprct-data}
data(HELPrct)

# Two-way contingency table of counts
tally_counts <- tally(substance ~ homeless, data = HELPrct)
tally_counts

# Conditional proportions by substance
tally(~ homeless | substance, format = "proportion", data = HELPrct)
```

### Hypothesis Test: Chi-Square Test of Independence
- $H_0$: Primary substance choice and housing status are independent.
- $H_a$: Primary substance choice and housing status are not independent.

```{r helprct-chisq}
xchisq.test(tally_counts)
```

### Conclusion
Because the $p$-value ($0.000202$) is far below $\alpha = 0.05$, we reject $H_0$. There is strong evidence that primary substance choice and housing status are dependent. Detoxification unit patients with alcohol dependency are significantly more likely to be homeless ($\approx 58.2\%$), whereas patients reporting cocaine ($\approx 38.8\%$) or heroin ($\approx 37.9\%$) use are more frequently housed.

## 2. Quantitative vs. Categorical I: Server Effect on Restaurant Bill Size

### Research Question
Is there a statistically significant difference in mean customer bill amounts across different servers at a dining establishment?

### Data & Summary
```{r tips-data}
data(RestaurantTips)

# Summary statistics by server
favstats(Bill ~ Server, data = RestaurantTips)
```

### Graphical Summaries & Assumption Checks
```{r tips-plots}
# Side-by-side boxplot
bwplot(Bill ~ Server, data = RestaurantTips, main = "Bill Amount by Server")

# Normal Q-Q plot for assumption verification
xqqmath(~ Bill | Server, data = RestaurantTips, main = "Normal Q-Q Plot: Bill by Server")
```

### Hypothesis Test: One-Way ANOVA
- $H_0: \mu_A = \mu_B = \mu_C$
- $H_a$: At least one server population mean bill is different.

```{r tips-anova}
aov_tips <- aov(Bill ~ Server, data = RestaurantTips)
summary(aov_tips)
```

### Conclusion
With an $F$-statistic of $1.671$ and $p$-value of $0.191 > 0.05$, we fail to reject $H_0$. There is insufficient evidence to conclude that mean customer bill amounts vary significantly across servers.

## 3. Quantitative vs. Categorical II: Commuting Time by Bicycle Frame Material

### Research Question
Are mean commuting travel times different depending on whether a carbon fiber or steel frame bicycle is used?

### Data & Summary
```{r bike-data}
data(BikeCommute)

# Summary statistics by bike frame
favstats(Minutes ~ Bike, data = BikeCommute)
```

### Graphical Summaries & Diagnostics
```{r bike-plots}
# Dotplot of commute minutes
gf_dotplot(~ Minutes | Bike, data = BikeCommute, title = "Commute Duration by Bike Frame")

# Boxplot
bwplot(Minutes ~ Bike, data = BikeCommute, main = "Commute Minutes by Bike Frame")

# Normal Q-Q plot
xqqmath(~ Minutes | Bike, data = BikeCommute, main = "Normal Q-Q Plot: Minutes by Bike")
```

### Hypothesis Test: Welch Two-Sample $t$-Test
- $H_0: \mu_{\text{carbon}} - \mu_{\text{steel}} = 0$
- $H_a: \mu_{\text{carbon}} - \mu_{\text{steel}} \ne 0$

```{r bike-ttest}
t.test(Minutes ~ Bike, data = BikeCommute, conf.level = 0.95)
```

### Conclusion
With $t = 0.3656$ and $p = 0.7163 > 0.05$, we fail to reject $H_0$. The data shows no statistically significant difference in mean commute time between carbon and steel frames. The 95% confidence interval for the mean difference is $[-2.49, 3.60]$ minutes.

## 4. Quantitative vs. Quantitative: MLB Team Wins and Runs Batted In

### Research Question
What is the relationship between regular season Major League Baseball team wins and Runs Batted In (RBIs)?

### Data & Scatterplot
```{r mlb-data}
data(BaseballHits2019)

# Scatterplot with fitted regression line
xyplot(Wins ~ RBI, type = c("p", "r"), data = BaseballHits2019,
       main = "2019 MLB Wins vs. Runs Batted In (RBI)", pch = 19, col = "navy")
```

### Correlation & Linear Model
```{r mlb-model}
# Correlation
r_val <- cor(Wins ~ RBI, data = BaseballHits2019)
cat("Correlation (r):", round(r_val, 4), "\n")
cat("R-squared:", round(r_val^2, 4), "\n")

# Linear model
lm_base <- lm(Wins ~ RBI, data = BaseballHits2019)
summary(lm_base)
```

### Conclusion
We reject $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ ($t = 7.507, p = 3.55 \times 10^{-8} < 0.001$). Team RBIs exhibit a strong, statistically significant positive linear relationship with team wins. The fitted regression equation is $\widehat{\text{Wins}} = -30.82 + 0.149 \times \text{RBI}$, explaining approximately $66.8\%$ of the variance in regular season wins.
